t: The fighting began over a Meccan caravan from the Levant, but the caravan escaped by another route and the two armies met at Badr anyway.
The only account of the battle is the Islamic tradition, written down some time later, and some histories doubt how much beyond it can be established.
Islamic tradition holds that angels took part and that the victory was divine; other sources attribute it to Muhammad's strategy.
dyk: The Qur'an calls the battle Yawm al-Furqan, 'The Day of the Criterion', and Ibn Ishaq's biography of Muhammad includes a complete name by name roster of the Muslim army.
ev: The Hijra: Muhammad and his followers migrate to Medina, where the community chooses him as leader
Early in the year Muhammad learns of a Meccan caravan returning from the Levant and gathers a force of around 300 men to intercept it
Abu Sufyan sends word to Mecca and changes the caravan's route; the Quraysh assemble an army
The Muslim army camps at the wells of Badr on 12 March, and the Quraysh march into the valley at midnight on 13 March
On 13 March the battle opens with duels and then a Meccan charge, and the Muslim counter-attack breaks the Meccan lines
About 70 prisoners are taken and, on Abu Bakr's advice, mostly released for ransom
Muhammad marches into Mecca, whose peaceful surrender Abu Sufyan helps to negotiate

f.place: Near the city of Badr, Medina Province, in present-day Saudi Arabia, in a valley between sand dunes and hills
f.sides: Muhammad's army of 313 to 317 men (313 is the generally accepted figure, with two horses and 70 camels) against a Qurayshi army led by Amr ibn Hisham, given as nearly one thousand or as around 1,300 men, with 100 horses
f.outcome: The Medinan army broke the Meccan lines; scholars estimate about 70 Meccan dead, 14 known Muslim dead and some 70 prisoners.
